```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
has_engine <- requireNamespace("flexyBayes", quietly = TRUE) &&
  requireNamespace("INLA", quietly = TRUE)
```

```{r setup}
library(pollinatoR)
```

## A second engine

`pollin_fit()` fits with glmmTMB by default. With `engine = "flexyBayes"` it
fits the same model as a Bayesian mixed model, through the flexyBayes package
on INLA. Estimates and intervals then come from posterior draws, which carry
the uncertainty in the variance components as well as in the fixed effects.
The rest of the package takes those draws as it takes the glmmTMB ones:
effects, populations, values and guards work unchanged.

In planted-truth simulations the posterior 95% intervals cover close to 95%
on designs with unit intercepts and on binomial counts. On designs with a
random treatment slope and 12 sites they cover about 91% to 93%. An exact
posterior computed by Stan gives the same coverage there, so the shortfall
comes from the interval itself with few sites. The package NEWS gives the
full results.

This vignette fits one simulated trial on both engines and compares the
results: the overall effect, its value, and the effect in each variety.

`r if (!has_engine) "flexyBayes and INLA are not installed where this page was built, so the code that needs them is shown without its results. Install both packages to run it."`

## Installing the engine

Neither package is on CRAN. flexyBayes installs from GitHub, and INLA from its
own repository.

```{r install, eval = FALSE}
# install.packages("remotes")
remotes::install_github("AAGI-AUS/flexyBayes")
install.packages(
  "INLA",
  repos = c(getOption("repos"), INLA = "https://inla.r-inla-download.org/R/stable"),
  dependencies = TRUE
)
```

The engine is checked when a fit is made. Without both packages,
`engine = "flexyBayes"` stops with a message naming the one that is missing.

## A simulated trial

Eight canola varieties are grown in six blocks. In every block each variety
has bagged plants, closed to insects, and open plants. The response is the
number of pods per plant. Varieties differ in how much they gain from insect
visits: each has its own treatment effect on the log scale, drawn around a
mean of 0.4.

```{r data}
set.seed(2026)
varieties <- sprintf("V%d", 1:8)
blocks <- sprintf("B%d", 1:6)
trial <- expand.grid(
  plant = 1:3,
  trt = c("Bagged", "Open"),
  block = blocks,
  variety = varieties,
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)
block_effect <- setNames(rnorm(6, 0, 0.2), blocks)
variety_effect <- setNames(rnorm(8, 0, 0.2), varieties)
variety_slope <- setNames(rnorm(8, 0.4, 0.25), varieties)
log_mu <- 3 + block_effect[trial$block] + variety_effect[trial$variety] +
  variety_slope[trial$variety] * (trial$trt == "Open")
trial$pods <- rnbinom(nrow(trial), mu = exp(log_mu), size = 15)
nrow(trial)

pd <- pollin_data(trial, response = "pods", treatment = "trt", unit = "block")
ds <- pollin_design(pd, arms = c(excluded = "Bagged", open = "Open"), layout = "rcbd")
est <- pollin_estimand(ds, "dependence", "ratio", "loss")
```

The planted loss share of each variety is `1 - exp(-slope)`:

```{r planted}
planted <- 1 - exp(-variety_slope)
round(planted, 2)
```

## The same model on both engines

The fixed part and the random terms are the same on both engines: the
treatment as a fixed effect and a random intercept per block. A negative
binomial family is set explicitly, so both engines use it.

```{r options, eval = has_engine}
# One INLA fit per model instead of the best of three.
options(flexyBayes.inla_best_of = 1L, flexyBayes.silence_default_prior_note = TRUE)
```

```{r fit-tmb}
fit_tmb <- pollin_fit(est, family = glmmTMB::nbinom2())
```

```{r fit-fb, eval = has_engine}
fit_fb <- pollin_fit(est, engine = "flexyBayes", family = glmmTMB::nbinom2())
fit_fb
```

`pollin_effects()` reads the loss share from each fit. On glmmTMB the interval
is the delta interval, taken over the fixed and random effects jointly. On
flexyBayes it is the posterior interval: the
estimate is the median of the posterior draws of the loss share, the interval
their equal-tailed 95% interval, and `p.value` is `NA`.

```{r effects-tmb}
eff_tmb <- pollin_effects(fit_tmb)
eff_tmb$table[, c("estimate", "std.error", "conf.low", "conf.high", "interval")]
```

```{r effects-fb, eval = has_engine}
eff_fb <- pollin_effects(fit_fb, n_draws = 1000L, seed = 1L)
rbind(eff_tmb$table, eff_fb$table)[
  , c("estimate", "std.error", "conf.low", "conf.high", "interval")
]
```

With a few hundred plants and a block intercept as the only random term, the
two engines agree closely. Both intervals carry the uncertainty in the block
variance: the posterior integrates over it, and the delta interval
approximates it through the joint precision of the Laplace approximation.

## From posterior draws to a value

On a flexyBayes fit, `pollin_draws()` uses `method = "posterior"`, its only
method there. Each draw takes the fixed effects, the block effects and the
variance parameters jointly from the posterior, and the two arm means are
recomputed from them. A seed sets both R's random number generator and INLA's,
so the draws repeat exactly.

```{r draws, eval = has_engine}
dr_fb <- pollin_draws(fit_fb, n = 1000L, method = "posterior", seed = 1L)
dr_fb
```

The draws go into `pollin_value()` exactly as simulation draws do. The market
inputs below are illustrative.

```{r value, eval = has_engine}
canola <- pollin_market(
  quantity = 3600,
  price = 700,
  unit = "t",
  currency = "AUD",
  year = 2025,
  source = "Illustrative inputs",
  crop = "canola"
)
dr_tmb <- pollin_draws(fit_tmb, n = 1000L, seed = 1L)
rbind(
  summary(pollin_value(dr_tmb, canola, channel = "dependence")),
  summary(pollin_value(dr_fb, canola, channel = "dependence"))
)[, c("median", "conf.low", "conf.high", "currency", "method")]
```

The vignette *From dependence to value* covers the channels, populations and
the double-count guard. Each of them takes posterior draws.

## The effect in each variety

The varieties were planted with different loss shares. There are two ways to
estimate them.

The unpooled way fits a separate treatment effect for each variety, as a
fixed interaction, with `pollin_fit(by = "variety")`, and reads them with
`pollin_effects()`. Each variety's estimate uses only that variety's plants.

```{r unpooled}
fit_by <- pollin_fit(est, family = glmmTMB::nbinom2(), by = "variety")
unpooled <- pollin_effects(fit_by)$table
```

The pooled way gives the varieties a random intercept and a random treatment
slope, with `pollin_fit(pooled = "variety")`, and reads the effect at each
level with `pollin_cate()`. A variety whose estimate is uncertain, or far from
the rest, is pulled towards the overall effect. A slope on a unit column, such
as site in a multi-site study, is declared in the design with
`pollin_design(slope = )` instead.

```{r pooled-tmb}
fit_pool_tmb <- pollin_fit(est, family = glmmTMB::nbinom2(), pooled = "variety")
cate_tmb <- pollin_cate(fit_pool_tmb, n = 1000L, seed = 1L)
```

```{r pooled-fb, eval = has_engine}
fit_pool_fb <- pollin_fit(
  est,
  engine = "flexyBayes",
  family = glmmTMB::nbinom2(),
  pooled = "variety"
)
cate_fb <- pollin_cate(fit_pool_fb, n = 1000L, seed = 1L)
cate_fb
```

The print keeps the two kinds apart: the table holds the pooled contrasts,
and a line points to the unpooled ones. Set side by side with the planted
values:

```{r compare-tmb}
compare <- data.frame(
  variety = varieties,
  planted = round(planted, 2),
  unpooled = round(unpooled$estimate, 2),
  pooled_glmmTMB = round(cate_tmb$table$estimate, 2)
)
compare
```

```{r compare-fb, eval = has_engine}
compare$pooled_flexyBayes <- round(cate_fb$table$estimate, 2)
compare
```

Pooling pulls the extreme varieties inwards: V1 rises on both engines, and
V2 and V7 fall. This does not bring every variety closer to its planted
value. V1 was planted with a negative loss share and moves away from it,
while V7 moves towards it. Partial pooling lowers the error over the
varieties as a whole, not for each one.

The two engines differ in how they get the interval. On flexyBayes it comes
from the posterior draws, as for the overall effect. On glmmTMB it is
approximate: the fixed effects and the varieties' slopes are drawn jointly
from a normal distribution with the covariance of the delta interval, so the
draws carry the correlation between them.

```{r intervals-tmb}
cate_tmb$table[, c("level", "estimate", "conf.low", "conf.high")]
```

In this trial they come out wider than the unpooled delta intervals,
although pooling should narrow them. The flexyBayes intervals are as narrow
as the unpooled ones or narrower.

When glmmTMB estimates the slope variance at zero, every variety's pooled
effect equals the overall one, and the conditional variances carry no
information. `pollin_cate()` stops on such a fit rather than report
intervals; the unpooled contrasts or the flexyBayes engine remain.

## What the engine refuses

The flexyBayes engine refuses, by name, what it cannot fit faithfully.

flexyBayes can also fit with brms, but the posterior draws of a brms fit are
not part of version 1 of the flexyBayes extension API, which is what
`pollinatoR` reads. The brms backend is refused:

```{r refuse-brms, eval = has_engine, error = TRUE}
try(pollin_fit(est, engine = "flexyBayes", backend = "brms"))
```

Five families are mapped to their flexyBayes counterparts on INLA:
`nbinom2()` (as `negative_binomial`), `poisson()`, `binomial()`,
`Gamma(link = "log")` (as `gamma`) and `beta_family()` (as `beta`), each with
its log or logit link. Any other family, such as Tweedie, is refused:

```{r refuse-tweedie, eval = has_engine, error = TRUE}
try(pollin_fit(est, engine = "flexyBayes", family = glmmTMB::tweedie()))
```

flexyBayes on INLA does not fit a correlated random treatment slope, the
unstructured slope that glmmTMB fits as `(trt | variety)`. The flexyBayes
route fits a variety intercept plus an independent effect for each
variety-by-arm cell instead. That is a restricted form of the unstructured
slope: the variance is the same in both arms and the correlation between
arms cannot be negative. The pooled effects on the two engines therefore come
from slightly different models, and where the true arms vary unequally
between varieties they can disagree for that reason alone.

## Priors

Priors are passed to `flexyBayes::flexybayes()` through `...` as written,
in the flexyBayes prior language of `flexyBayes::fb_prior()`. `pollinatoR`
adds no priors of its own. Without one, flexyBayes uses its default, a
half-normal prior on each random-effect standard deviation and a nearly flat
prior on the fixed effects. Here the treatment coefficient, the log of the
open-to-bagged ratio, gets a normal prior with standard deviation 1:

```{r prior, eval = has_engine}
fit_prior <- pollin_fit(
  est,
  engine = "flexyBayes",
  family = glmmTMB::nbinom2(),
  prior = flexyBayes::fb_prior(b("trtOpen") ~ normal(mean = 0, sd = 1))
)
pollin_effects(fit_prior, n_draws = 1000L, seed = 1L)$table[
  , c("estimate", "conf.low", "conf.high")
]
```

`flexyBayes::prior_summary()` on a fitted model, `fit_prior$fits$pods`, lists
each prior and the INLA parameter it reached.
